checks: If all negative coefficients are −1 after dropping zeros, the capped positive sum has the integer total equal to their number and the half-mass theorem applies. Otherwise a free negative exists; the free-pair theorem bounds the number of free positives by one. With no free positive the positives are all units; with one p<1 the total positive mass is at least one, so there is also a positive unit.

The latter case supplies at least two positive phases, a negative phase and a free phase of each sign. As in the free-pair proof, two-sided free-coordinate transfers force a common derivative qf(0), and the supporting tangent for log f on one half-line plus integrability gives 0<q<1.

At each free negative magnitude the reciprocal transform has the same level 1/q and positive derivative. If two magnitudes b_1<b_2 had that level, convexity gives ψ_−(b_2)≥ψ_−(b_1)+(b_2−b_1)ψ_−′(b_1)>ψ_−(b_1), a contradiction.

At an additional −1, the tangent at b gives ψ_−(1)>ψ_−(b) and hence a smaller signed derivative. Increasing this extra coefficient while decreasing p is a feasible one-sided descent, with a_0 fixed. At a zero coordinate the signed derivative equals f(0)>qf(0); increasing p and decreasing the zero is also a feasible descent. The ambient differentiability in the accepted lemma includes both boundary directions.

Balance gives mb=k+p−1. From p>0 and b<1, m>mb>k−1, so the integer m is at least k. There are exactly k+m+2 coordinates, including the fixed −1 and the fractional positive, giving k+m=d−1. The three forms need not be disjoint, and no converse is asserted.
